storySnapshots.class_notes: Use the Library test below to ask which capability a benchmark measured and whether it matches the result you need. Background: AI Fundamentals 101 §12.5 — Evals: Custom Tests for Your Specific Needs.
storySnapshots.cocktail_party: “A correct answer does not finish the work of understanding it.”
storySnapshots.headline: Leading mathematicians say a correct answer is not the whole job

heroVisual.alt: An illustrated notebook shows 100 × 0.25 = 25 above a square divided into four parts with one quarter shaded.

storySnapshots.laidies_read:
A benchmark is a defined test used to compare performance on a chosen task. A correct proof may still require people to identify its useful idea, connect earlier work and explain it.

In an ETH Zurich interview, declaration signatory Alessio Figalli said AI can accelerate results, especially where established methods and literature exist. His concern is that faster output can outrun the slower work of judging which results matter and training people to formulate good questions. That is his assessment, not a settled measure of what AI understands.

sources.label: ETH Zurich — interview with Alessio Figalli

storySnapshots.the_story:
Twenty-five recipients of the Fields Medal, a leading mathematics award, published a September 11 declaration. They argue that using mathematical problem-solving as an AI benchmark can pull attention from explanation, attribution, discussion and teaching.

This is an attributed argument, not evidence that AI cannot produce correct mathematics or a rule for researchers or students.
storySnapshots.what_this_means:
The distinction matters in ordinary learning. If an AI solves a percentage problem for you, the displayed answer finishes one task. Your learning has a different test: can you explain each step, notice a bad assumption and solve a changed version without copying the first response?

Try a small two-pass check. First ask the AI for a solution. Then hide it and explain the method in your own words. Change one number or condition and solve again. Compare your reasoning with the original. The point is not to reject the tool; it is to check whether the answer became knowledge you can use.

storySnapshots.cocktail_party: “After the ad click, you’re chatting with the seller.”
storySnapshots.headline: A new ChatGPT ad can open a separate conversation with the seller

heroVisual.alt: An illustrated tablet shows two separate blank chat panels beside a desk lamp and a measuring tape.

storySnapshots.laidies_read: “Sponsored” tells you who is paying for the conversation. You are talking to a seller about what it offers, through an AI agent inside ChatGPT. That is useful context: a fluent answer can still be part of a sales conversation.
storySnapshots.the_story:
OpenAI announced September 16 that it is testing Sponsored Agents with select US advertisers. After clicking an ad in ChatGPT, a person can choose to open a clearly labelled conversation with an agent sponsored by that business.

OpenAI says the sponsored conversation is separate from the person’s original chat and from ChatGPT’s independent answers. The announcement does not give broader availability details.
storySnapshots.what_this_means:
Imagine an ad for a desk lamp catches your eye. In the separate conversation, ask for its base width, shade height and return terms. Then compare those claims with the product page before deciding whether it fits your bedside table.

The important hand-off happens when you click the ad and choose the new conversation. Pause there long enough to notice the label and who is speaking. Keep the original answer, the sponsored conversation and the seller’s product page as three different sources.
